#8837. The 67-Year-Old Who Raced Two Full Ironmans a Week Apart

Mary Mitchell won her age group in Kona and eight days later raced Ironman California, where she also won her age group. Here's how she did it. (Photo: Mary Mitchell, FinisherPix)

Fresh off a sixth-place finish at the Ironman World Championship in Kona, American professional triathlete Sam Long recently took to Instagram to ask his followers a question. Should he race Ironman Florida on November 7, or give himself another two weeks to recover and race Ironman Cozumel on November 22?

Long wants to secure his qualification for the 2027 Ironman World Championship early, but the question of how quickly to return to racing after Kona is a serious one. Among the responses to his post were plenty of suggestions that he take the extra recovery time and race Cozumel instead.

After all, Kona is no ordinary Ironman. Its combination of heat, humidity, unpredictable winds and exposed terrain takes a major physical toll, even on athletes who have spent their careers preparing for those conditions. Racing another Ironman just four weeks later is ambitious enough. What about racing one eight days later?

For 67-year-old Australian age-grouper Mary Mitchell, that was precisely the challenge.

On October 10, Mitchell won the women’s 65-69 age group at the Ironman World Championship in Kona, finishing in 13:11:46. Eight days later, she lined up at Ironman California in Sacramento, where she crossed the finish line in 11:32:45, more than 90 minutes faster than her Kona performance.

And she won her age group again. Even more remarkably, her husband, Andrew, 66, who had also raced in Kona, joined her in Sacramento and won his age group too.

What began as a somewhat improbable endurance experiment ended with three age-group victories between them.

The idea wasn’t actually Mary’s. Earlier this year, Mary and Andrew traveled to Morocco to spend time altitude training in the Atlas Mountains with a friend. During the trip, their friend floated an intriguing challenge. What would happen if a bunch of athletes in their 60s attempted two full-distance Ironmans a week apart?

“He persuaded us that it would be a good human experiment to do, to see whether, at our age, you could do two Ironmans in eight days, and what would that be like?” Mitchell explains.

The plan was for all three to qualify for Kona, race the World Championship, and then travel to Sacramento for Ironman California the following weekend.

There was just one problem. Their friend subsequently suffered a knee injury and withdrew from the experiment. But Mary and Andrew had already committed. Their flights and accommodation were booked and the race entries paid for.

“We thought, well, we might as well go,” Mitchell recalls. “How bad can it be?”

They also had the encouragement – or perhaps bad influence – of American friends Jill and Dougin Walker, serial Ironman competitors who have completed around 100 Ironmans apiece.

“We’ve fallen in with a bad crowd,” she jokes.

For Mitchell, who has completed around 30 Ironmans since her first in 2004, racing twice in eight days was uncharted territory. The closest she had previously come was roughly a month between Kona and Ironman Malaysia.

But Mitchell also had another reason to make the most of Kona.

Mitchell had previously won her age group at the Ironman World Championship in 2019. Since then, however, her attempts to return to the top of the podium had been repeatedly derailed.

In 2022, she was hit by a car while riding on the Queen Ka’ahumanu Highway just 10 days prior, preventing her from starting the race.

In 2024, at the women’s World Championship in Nice, she developed food poisoning the night before the race and abandoned roughly 140 kilometers into the bike.

Then in 2025, she returned to Kona, only to discover that what she initially believed to be a cold was COVID. She struggled throughout the race and eventually withdrew on the run.

“I had three years of thwarted attempts to do the World Championship,” she says.

Heading into 2026, Mitchell and her husband had decided this would be their final Kona appearance. They wanted to experience other races and destinations rather than continue returning to the Big Island.

And for much of the race day, Mitchell’s final Kona appearance looked unlikely to deliver another world title.

Mitchell had hoped to swim around 90 minutes, but the ocean conditions and what she admits was insufficient swim preparation conspired against her. She eventually emerged from Kailua Bay in 1:57:06.

“I had an appalling swim,” she says. “I hadn’t done enough long swimming, didn’t have enough endurance, just because swimming’s not my favorite thing.”

By the time she reached transition, Mitchell had effectively written off her chances of winning: “When I stood up out of the water, I thought, a competitive race is off the table now.”

Rather than chase positions, she decided to enjoy what she believed would be her last Ironman World Championship. Her mantra became simple: “Look after yourself and just keep chipping away at it.”

Despite the heat, wind, and particularly oppressive humidity, Mitchell began making steady progress through the field. She completed the bike in 6:38:10 and started the marathon feeling surprisingly good. She settled into a sustainable pace, making sure to take in adequate fluids and calories at every aid station.

With her husband, Andrew, also competing, there was nobody on the sidelines feeding her information about her position. It wasn’t until she reached the top of the Energy Lab, with roughly 12 kilometers remaining, that an acquaintance delivered some unexpected news.

“She said, ‘You’re first and running faster than anyone else in your age group.’ And I’m like, ‘What? No, come on.’”

Mitchell completed the marathon in 4:23:23, the fastest run in her age group, to secure her second age-group world title.

Ordinarily, the next few days would have been devoted to celebrating, recovering and enjoying the satisfaction of a long-awaited victory. Instead, she had another Ironman looming.

Following the Kona awards dinner and a celebratory glass of wine, Mary and Andrew flew to Sacramento, arriving on Monday with less than a week remaining before their next race.

There was no elaborate recovery protocol, no special preparation, and definitely no attempt to squeeze in additional fitness.

“We rode our bikes for an hour to an hour and a half along the river trail a couple of times, which was really nice,” Mitchell recalls.

The rides were deliberately easy, simply turning their legs over while enjoying the scenery and wildlife. She also completed a couple of short runs no longer than 30 minutes or demanding.

Her only swim was a brief dip in the river to test the water temperature and a new wetsuit, purchased after her previous one split during a 70.3 race in Leipzig, Germany, earlier in the trip.

More surprisingly, Mitchell wasn’t experiencing any crippling muscle soreness she remembered from her earlier Ironman days.

“It’s strange. They sort of ached, but they didn’t actually feel sore,” she explains.

She believes advances in running shoe technology have made a meaningful difference to how her legs feel after an Ironman. She raced in “super shoes” but suspects recovering from back-to-back marathons would have been considerably harder in the shoes available a decade ago.

Still, there was plenty of uncertainty. When asked whether she questioned the wisdom of attempting another Ironman, Mary laughs: “Oh, I thought about that just about every day.”

“If they’d had a half [Ironman] race, I probably would have dropped down to that distance.”

She reasoned that California’s current-assisted, wetsuit-legal swim would be far less demanding than Kona’s ocean swim. The flat, relatively straightforward bike course also appeared manageable.

But the marathon was another matter entirely.

“My big concern throughout the whole week was the run. Can you do two marathons in eight days with having raced in Kona with the conditions that are notoriously one of the more difficult races that you can do?”

Mitchell had trained specifically for Kona and made no adjustments to prepare for the double. Whatever happened in Sacramento would simply happen.

As expected, the California swim was a very different experience. Thanks to the river current and wetsuit, Mitchell emerged from the water in approximately 55 minutes, effectively halving her swim time from Kona.

But the bike wasn’t entirely without incident. Early in the ride, Mitchell developed significant pain in her quadriceps muscle and her shin. By the end of the first 90-kilometer lap, she was seriously considering pulling out.

“I was thinking, should I stop? It’s really quite sore,” she recalls. “Am I causing damage?”

She decided to continue to the next aid station and reassess, knowing she could stop at any point. Eventually, the pain subsided.

With no expectations, and already holding her Kona qualification for the following year, Mitchell approached the rest of the race with an unusually relaxed attitude. She chatted with volunteers, stopped when necessary, and enjoyed the atmosphere.

“I was just chilled the entire race because I didn’t have anything to prove,” she explains.

The marathon, her greatest concern, proved surprisingly manageable. Rather than experiencing the crushing fatigue she had anticipated, Mitchell found herself settling into a rhythm. The crowds were enthusiastic, the aid stations welcoming, and she passed the kilometers chatting with other competitors.

Her marathon time, 4:23:30, was almost identical to the one she had run in Kona eight days earlier. When she crossed the finish line in 11:32:45, she had not only completed the experiment but had also won her age group again. Andrew had done the same.

“To our astonishment, we both won our age groups,” Mitchell says.

Perhaps even more surprising was how they felt afterward.

“When we first started this sport, you do an Ironman and basically couldn’t walk for three days. Getting up out of a chair was really difficult and painful.”

This time, within 24 to 48 hours, both felt remarkably normal.

Mitchell discovered triathlon in her 30s, partly because Andrew was already involved in sport and she was tired of being left at home while he trained. She bought a cheap bike, started entering local short-course events and quickly fell in love with the sport and its community.

Her first Ironman came in 2004 at Busselton in Western Australia. Like many newcomers, she initially assumed it would be a one-off experience. More than two decades later, she’s still going.

Now retired and living in Adelaide, Mitchell trains up to 20-25 hours per week during her biggest blocks. She has worked with a coach for many years and increasingly recognizes the importance of strength training and nutrition, particularly in preserving muscle mass as she ages. Around five years ago, she also began working with a sports dietitian to improve her fueling, gut training, and overall nutritional approach.

But Mitchell is quick to point out that endurance sport doesn’t consume her entire existence. She enjoys good food, wine, socializing, reading and traveling with Andrew. And while she is competitive, she says curiosity is an even greater motivation.

“I just want to see how far I can push myself,” she explains.

Since retiring, Mitchell has challenged herself to do “at least one thing each year that takes me out of my comfort zone.”

Last year, that meant racing Patagonman in Chile, confronting her dislike of cold water by jumping from a ferry into a freezing cold fjord to start the race. This year, it was the Kona-California double. Next year, she’s already entered the 100-kilometer Tarawera ultramarathon in New Zealand.

For Mitchell, the biggest reward of the double wasn’t another age-group victory. It was discovering that, at age 67, she could still surprise herself.

“I think it resets your mind. It resets your thinking about what your body can achieve. And what mentally you can achieve,” she reflects.

The experience also reinforced what she loves about triathlon: the places it takes her, the friendships it creates, and the opportunities to challenge assumptions about her own limitations.

“It’s taught me that you’re stronger than you think you are, mentally and physically.”

Would she ever attempt two Ironmans in eight days again?

“No. Absolutely not. There’s no need to repeat the experiment!”

For all the satisfaction of the achievement, Mitchell admits she would have liked more time to savor her second Kona world title. Instead, almost immediately, she was packing up and preparing to race again.

“It would have been nice to just chill and enjoy it a little bit more,” she explains. “Have a couple more glasses of wine, soak it in.”

But the experience did change one thing: Despite initially declaring that 2026 would be their last Kona, Mary and Andrew have both accepted qualifying slots to next year’s World Championship.

#8835. How Yoga Brings You Closer to Yourself and the Life You Want

If you buy through our links, we may earn an affiliate commission. This supports our mission to get more people active and outside.Learn about Outside Online's affiliate link policy

In Yoga Journal’s Archives series, we share a curated collection of articles originally published in past issues beginning in 1975. This article about yoga as a science and an art first appeared in the January-February 1977 issue of Yoga Journal. Find more of our Archives here.

Yoga is a science, an art, and a technique which spans the multilevel functioning of the individual. It is a science because of its empirical approach, presented most completely by the classic Yoga Sutras of Patanjali at least 1,000 years ago. Science is defined as a methodology which requires empirical proof of its theories; it requires that which proves a theory be easily repeatable by another experimenter if he/she follows the rules of the experiment.

Yoga, by this definition, is indeed a science. Its rules are given in sutra form and the presentation of Patanjali is a “how-to” book of the highest order. The practitioner need only follow the lead of Patanjali in order to have his own personal empirical results. (It is true that the directions are in parts esoteric and apparently illusive; this points out the necessity of having a teacher upon whom the practioner can rely for advice during certain intervals.) In addition to the work by Patanjali, the Hatha Yoga Pradipika and the Gheranda and Shiva Samhita are references which can explain the science of yoga.

But yoga is an art, too. Individuals have dedicated their lives to the perfection of this art. This does not necessarily imply the production of tangible output such as texts, although these have been produced in the history of traditional Indian thought. Rather, the use of the word “art” in this context implies the movement toward perfection within, the embodiment of beauty as it can be expressed through the human being. If one dedicates his/her life to the art of yoga, this implies a dedication which does not involve merely daily practice numbering a few hours. Instead, it implies a minute by minute practice which spans years, and some believe, lifetimes of existence.

The art of yoga is the practice of yoga on all levels of existence; this means every thought, action, dream, relationship, food intake, sexual activity, occupation, etc., are brought into the wider perspective of observation in light of the individual’s desire to understand the Self. This understanding does not imply intellectual understanding alone. It implies the “living” or the “being” in the Self rather than just mentally knowing about the Self. One can compare this to the experience of being in a hurricane with merely reading about the experience of a hurricane; the effect would be quite different.

One who lives in the Self has come into a wholeness of being, possibly for us all by virtue of our human existence, but available presently to only a handful due a complex interplay of events which, for whatever reasons, has brought them to a newer threshold of consciousness. Thus the art of yoga lies in bringing perfection into action through becoming one with oneself.

Part of the ability to do this lies with the powerful psychological technique of “acting as if.” If one wishes to meditate, one often begins by acting as if one were meditating. As the form of meditation is assumed, the content of meditation begins to be experienced. If one acts as if one loves another, and acts with sincerity and with honesty, often feelings of love toward that person do begin to flow. So with yoga. If one watches and practices as if yoga were an art and the Self were the artist, then this lends validity to the possibility of this being true.

This brings one to the question of technique. Yoga is also a concrete way of bringing about profound physical, mental, emotional, and spiritual changes within the individual. The student is instructed in yama and niyama (basic ethical precepts), in asanas (meditative postures), in pranayama (conscious voluntary control of the energy associated with breath), in pratyhara and dharana (watching and observing the mind), and finally, in dhyana, or meditation. The final experiencing of samadhi (union) cannot be taught; it is both the result of the foregoing disciplines and independent of them. The understanding of this apparent paradox is part of the process of learning about yoga.

Thus yoga can be seen from the angles of science, art or technique. It can be approached as a small practice of one’s life, or as the way that life is lived, a quality which is brought to live which liberates one from the strong bonds of ego.

#8831. Triathlon Gear Our Editors Used and Loved in October 2026

If you buy through our links, we may earn an affiliate commission. This supports our mission to get more people active and outside.Learn about Outside Online's affiliate link policy

It’s officially the off-season. In Ohio, we’re having the best fall, where no one complains about the weather (rare for Ohioans) and no wind or rain storms have blown through, robbing us of the vibrant change in the leaves. Hiking is a staple way to enjoy the crunchy leaves, swimming has moved fully indoors, and biking has a sort of leisure to it that it doesn’t have when the landscape is green.

As we slow down and explore other outdoor hobbies in the coming months, here’s a look at the gear our editors are reaching for.

This might seem like an unusual choice for a triathlete, but as the race season winds down and we transition from workouts to just-getting-out, I find myself blasting all of my tempo trainers to the back of my closet in favor of this pair of Jeep-wheel-level all-terrain crushers. For those unfamiliar with Norda, the Canadian brand hit the scene in 2021 (bad timing, sorry) with the release of their ultra-premium — read: ultra-expensive — $285 shoe dubbed the 001. Folks had a field day with the high price, but few could deny that the 001 was something different than what was out there already.

Fast forward to today, and Norda is still (crazy) expensive, but they also still offer shoes that are entirely novel in the increasingly crowded trail running shoe world. The 055 was released earlier this summer as a maximal take on the well-loved, but race-focused 005. For me, I love how you can point your foot at literally anything and the thick-but-stable base will eat it up. Better yet, the woven gaiter adds another layer of stability and protection, meaning you don’t really have to think much about where you put your feet, allowing me to, quite simply, zone out and enjoy the view. And that’s what fall “training” is all about, anyway.

Winter is coming, which in Phoenix means two things: socks come out of storage, and they better be day-glo. Because I live and train downtown, where traffic is abundant and drivers are always (always!) distracted, I dress as obnoxiously as possible to make sure they see me. That means neon fabrics, reflective materials, and LED lights on as many points as possible.

Years ago, I interviewed a safety expert who said you especially want these materials on the parts of your body that move he most when you ride or run, as movement is more likely to catch the eye of a driver. These bright socks have reflective yarn woven into the fabric, making my legs easier to spot on rides and runs. They’re comfortable, they stay up, and they stand up to multiple runs and laundry cycles each week.

Do I look like a 90s fever dream in my neon wardrobe? I sure do. But you’ll see me coming from a mile away, and that’s the whole point.

I haven’t had long hair in the 14 years I’ve been a triathlete — until now. I hate the feeling of hair skimming my neck or swishing back and forth as I run, so it has to be all the way up in the ugliest messy bun. Basically, I’m the opposite of Marjolaine Pierré.

I found that the Goody ComforFlex holds my hair well without pulling, no matter the intensity of workouts. And I don’t end up with tons of hair wrapped around them, which leads me to believe they are keeping my hair at least somewhat healthy despite regular chlorine exposure and frequent washes.

They’ve also held up well, so I can use the same one for at least a month before replacing it.

I’m ashamed to admit I’ve been one of *those* triathletes showing up at the local bike shop, frazzled and looking for the nearest mechanic, then frantically explaining how my seat clamp fell down my downtube and lodged itself somewhere seemingly impossible to reach. Yes, this happened to me at Ironman Chattanooga last year. As someone who prides myself on fixing my own bike issues, this was and still is my worst nightmare.

But I know I’m not alone. Between packing and trying to fit in final workouts ahead of travel, we triathletes can make some poor choices. Add to it that we’re limited in what tools we can bring to fix the problems we create, and it’s a recipe for disaster. Even when we have room and enough weight left to throw them in the bag, we often rush the pack job and toss them in without much organization.

After Chattanooga, I vowed to be more prepared. That’s when a friend showed me this trusty little roll-up tool bag that they use for camping. Small enough that it doesn’t take up all the room, big enough to fit what I need, and cheap enough to buy one for myself and a friend. It was the perfect recommendation.

And the best thing is you don’t have to travel for triathlon to get use out of it. Mine hangs in the garage when I’m home, and I use it every time I work on my bike.

— Travis Mundell, social media strategist

#8830. 15-Minute Beginner-Friendly Yoga, No Flexibility Required

Taylor Lorenz—known online as Taylor’s Tracks—is a certified yoga teacher with more than 800 hours of training in vinyasa, hatha, and yin yoga. Here, she guides you through a practice suitable for any experience level with yoga.

No matter how long you’ve been practicing yoga, returning to the basics is always beneficial. This yoga for beginners practice features a flow full of repeating shapes, including forward bends, side stretches, and gentle twists, all supported by modifications and props, if needed, to ensure that the poses work for any body, regardless of how flexible or inflexible you might be.

Listen to your body, breathe slowly, and enjoy the flow.

Keep two yoga blocks or block-like props (think: thick books) close by. These can help you access poses that your body might otherwise object to so that you can still benefit.

Begin kneeling in Thunderbolt Pose. If this doesn’t feel comfortable for your ankles or knees, slide a block beneath your sit bones to minimize the pressure. If it’s still uncomfortable, you can skip this pose.

Come onto your hands and knees with your shoulders over your wrists, hips stacked over your knees. With your next inhalation, lower your belly, lift your chin and chest, and arch your back in Cow Pose.

Exhale as you round your back and tuck your chin in Cat Pose.

Repeat Cat and Cow 3 times each, moving with the pace of your breath.

As you round into your last Cat Pose, tuck your toes and sink your sit bones back toward your heels.

Shift your shoulders forward over your wrists. Keep your toes tucked and with your next exhalation, lift your knees away from the mat and reach your hips up and back in Downward-Facing Dog. Think of your body being in an inverted V shape.

Feel free to bend you knees as much as you need to for the pose to feel comfortable along your hamstrings and lower back. You can also place blocks underneath your hands.

Stay here for 3 cycles of breath, pedaling out your feet by bending one knee and straightening the other, and then switching. You can also sway a little from side to side or simply stay in stillness.

Walk your feet toward your hands to come into a Standing Forward Bend. Relax your neck and let your head hang. You can let your hands dangle or rest your fingertips on the mat.

You can also place a block beneath each of your hands. You might want to bend your knees slightly to ease the strain on your hamstrings or lower back.

Inhale and start to lift your chest slightly, bringing your fingertips to your shins and lengthening your spine in Halfway Lift. Keep the back of your neck long and stare straight down at the mat. You can also keep your fingertips on your blocks here.

Inhale to rise as you come to standing, sweeping your arms out toward the sides and overhead. Bring your hands together at heart center in Mountain Pose.

With your next inhalation, reach your arms back toward the sky. Grab your left wrist with your right hand and guide your left wrist up and over to the right in a Standing Side Bend. Feel the stretch along your left side body.

Inhale as you come back through center and exhale as you twist toward the right, with your left arm reaching forward and your right arm reaching toward the back of the mat. Gaze toward the right.

When you’re ready, come back through center before repeating Standing Side Bend and Standing Twist on the opposite side.

Inhale to come back through center, exhale to Standing Forward Bend.

With your next exhalation, step back to Downward-Facing Dog.

From Downward Dog, step your right foot between your hands. Lower your left knee to the mat and sweep your arms overhead in Low Lunge.

Use our right hand to grab hold of your left wrist again, guiding it up and over in a side bend while keeping your balance in your Low Lunge. Press through your right foot and your back knee to help find steadiness.

Inhale as you come back through center and exhale as you twist toward the right, with your left arm reaching forward and your right arm reaching toward the back of the mat.

Inhale both arms back to center, palms facing forward. With your exhalation, bring your hands to the ground or to blocks on either side of your front foot. Start to straighten your front leg, sliding your right heel away from you and flexing your right foot in Half Splits.

You can keep your hands underneath your shoulders or slide them forward closer to your feet for a more intense shoulder and side body stretch.

With your next inhalation, come back through Low Lunge. Exhale, Downward-Facing Dog.

Reach your left leg to the sky and repeat the following poses on the opposite side:

Step toward the front of the mat and fold forward in Standing Forward Bend.

Inhale, reaching your arms up and overhead with your big toes touching or hip-distance apart. With your exhalation, reach your arms alongside your head and sit your hips back in Chair Pose.

Keep your arms high and begin to draw your left knee toward your chest, foot flexed. With your exhalation, step your left foot back into a High Lunge.

With your right hand, grab your left wrist, and reaching up and over toward the right side.

Inhale to come back through center. Exhale to open your arms toward the right, left arm forward, right arm back.

Inhale to reach both arms toward the sky. Exhale to straighten the right leg, hinging at your hips and folding your chest toward your right leg with your back heel lifted in a less intense variation of Pyramid Pose. Bring your hands to the mat to frame your front foot, your shin, or blocks on either side of your foot. Take 1 full breath here.

When you’re ready, step your left foot up to meet your right in Standing Forward Bend.

Inhale, reaching your arms up and overhead. With your exhalation, keep your arms high and sit your hips back in Chair Pose.

Repeat the following poses on the opposite side:

Gently land your knees to your mat and move through hands and knee into a seated position. Bring the soles of your feet together and let your knees fall out toward the sides in Bound Angle Pose. If this feels too intense, slide a blocks beneath each knee for extra support.

Stay here, or round your spine and walk your hands forward as you bring your chest toward your toes. Let your body find where it wants to be rather than force the shape. Take 5 breaths in your chosen position.

When you’re ready, move through a seated position to come all the way onto your back in Savasana. Feel free to add blocks beneath your knees for extra support.

Stay here for 3-5 minutes or as long as you’d like.

Push yourself upright to a comfortable seat. Bring your hands together at heart center, bow your head, and thank yourself for showing up on your mat today.

#8827. The Best Bike Lights for Triathletes in 2026, Tested and Reviewed

If you buy through our links, we may earn an affiliate commission. This supports our mission to get more people active and outside.Learn about Outside Online's affiliate link policy

Bottom Line: Each of the bike lights in our Best Bike Lights of 2026 list below has been tested on long rides by an experienced triathlete for many miles. Our reviewer is unbiased, with no brand relationships, meaning no brand has paid to appear in our list.

It’s that time of year again. You glance at your training plan, realize your post-work ride slot will now be taking place in the dark, and suddenly “bike light” jumps to the top of your shopping list. The good news is that bike lights in 2026 are significantly better than offerings from just a few years ago. You could even say they are light-years ahead (pun intended) of the bike lights from the 20th century. They are brighter, lighter, and – critically for triathletes – easier to mount on your bike than ever before.

But before you order the cheapest bike light on Amazon, there’s a bit more to think through. The cheapest option is far from the best, but you also don’t need to take out a second mortgage to buy a bike light either. Here’s what actually matters when buying lights as a triathlete, followed by the best options on the market right now.

As a light-toting triathlete, your goal isn’t just to see the road ahead of you; it is also to be seen. Public roads are far from perfectly safe, especially in today’s phone-addicted world filled with distracted drivers. But thankfully, having a bike light is one of the best ways to gain the attention of nearby drivers, reminding them to slow down and give you space as they pass by.

When shopping for a bike light, you want to consider two different design priorities, and pay close attention because most lights optimize for one or the other. First, you want a bike light that shines a powerful beam down the road, illuminating your path at speed in the dark. Second, you want a light that is designed to be seen. These lights use wide-angle optics, lateral emission, and attention-grabbing flash patterns to make you visible to cross-traffic and drivers approaching from the rear. Ideally, your bike light(s) do both.

For triathletes specifically, the lighting challenge runs deeper than a single unit on your bicycle. You might actually want three different lights for the corresponding sports. The ideal setup might include front and rear coverage on the bike, a headlamp or chest light for early-morning runs, and some form of visibility for open-water swims, especially those before sunrise. Each sport requires different hardware, but in this guide, we’ll focus on bike lights. Let’s help you figure out how to sort and sift through the hundreds of options on the market.

The standard brightness unit for sports lights is lumens. The higher the number, the brighter the light. But brighter isn’t always better. Some brands love to advertise max lumens at maximum output, but that can drain the battery in under two hours. Always check the light’s runtime at the mode you’ll actually use.

Consider the type of darkness you’ll be riding in, and how much light you’ll need. Not every triathlete will train in pitch darkness, so here is a quick reference of what you’ll find on the light market:

A pinpoint beam aimed straight ahead is great for one thing, and that’s seeing directly in front of you. But if you’re riding in the dark, you also want to have side visibility, not just from your own perspective, but for other riders and drivers to see you. The best bike lights have a wide spread beam that alerts drivers approaching from angles, not just head-on. Some lights now use multiple LEDs, which is worth considering if you ride in the dark year-round.

This is one of the most important aspects of a bike light because if the battery dies while you are riding in the dark 20 miles from home, you are SOL. Most bike lights are USB-C rechargeable, but runtime varies enormously. If you don’t get a light with a low-battery warning (ideally with several minutes of reserve before shutdown), make sure you keep tabs on how long you’ve been running it before it’s time to recharge.

This is where triathletes diverge from road cyclists. Aero bars, clip-on extensions, and non-standard cockpit shapes make standard clamp mounts useless in many setups. When shopping for lights, you’ll want to look for options that come with flexible silicone straps, GoPro-style mounts, or Garmin quarter-turn compatibility. Silicone straps cover the widest range of setups and are easy to transfer between bikes.

In the 2026 bike light market, there are a number of smart features that come with some of the more pristine options. Some of the features are just bells and whistles, but a few are genuinely helpful, especially for triathletes. Radar integration (Garmin Varia), ANT+ connectivity, automatic brightness adjustment, and brake-sensing technology are popular features that help improve function and safety on the bike. These are not marketing gimmicks – radar in particular can dramatically improve your confidence when riding on open roads with traffic.

Front light placement can be the trickiest part of lighting your tri bike. You can choose between below the basebar (the most aerodynamic option), midway down the aerobars (if the light rotates that direction), and arguably the best solution: adding a computer bridge to your aerobars and mounting the light on top or below it. Whatever you choose, test it on a bumpy road during daylight hours before relying on it in the dark. Remember that you’re not only looking for the light to stay attached, but also for the angle to remain stable as the light illuminates the road in front of you.

Rear lights are much more forgiving, with the seatpost being the most ideal spot for a rear-facing bike light. If you have limited seatpost access, you can mount a light on the seatstay. Just make sure your light is pointing backward rather than toward the sky or floor. If you have bottles or other gear mounted under or behind your seat, make sure they don’t block the bike light when they are fully loaded.

Output: 1,300 lumens front; 90 lumens rear

Battery life: 1.5 hrs front; 4.5 hrs rear

The Ion Pro and Flare bike lights do much more than illuminate through darkness. The paired set uses ANT+ to link the front and rear lights together, and you can control both from a compatible Garmin or Wahoo head unit. Up front, the Ion Pro has up to 1,300 lumens, which is more than enough for most low-light situations. It also has a clean beam pattern with solid front and side visibility, with a few hours of battery life across various power settings. In the rear, the Flare can be used with a 16-degree offset mount option that helps solve one of the most common triathlete problems: mounting a rear light on an angled seatpost or seatstay. The mount is sold separately, but it only costs $5.

Pros: ANT+ integration, offset rear mount solves tri-bike seatpost issues ($5 cost), strong front output Cons: Pricey for a set; front light only has 90 minutes of runtime at max output

Output: 130 to 1,000 lumens with six different modes

Battery life: 120 hrs on ECO FLASH; up to 2 hrs at max output

The Blinder has earned its spot on best-of lists for years, and the 2026 version is no exception. IP67 waterproofing and six different light modes make the Blinder 1000 suitable for a wide range of weather and light conditions, including midnight rain-riding. At low outputs, the Blinder 1000 lasts for days on a single charge. GoPro-style and standard handlebar mounts are both included, making it versatile on almost any tri cockpit.

Pros: Fully IP67 waterproof, versatile mounts, solid build quality, side window visibility

Cons: Heavier than some competitors at the same lumen output

Battery life: 1 hr at max output; up to 60 hrs at minimum output

If your friends call you “Nightrider,” then the AMPP 2200 might be the perfect bike light for you. With a max output of 2,200 lumens, the AMPP 2200 obliterates darkness in a way that can make you feel like you’re riding during the daytime. This is the light for those who ride in pitch darkness at speed, or those who live in extreme daylight climates such as Alaska or Iceland. While its top-end output is impressive, the AMPP 2200 includes different light modes that are ideal for riding in the dusk rather than the pitch black. At 500 to 800 lumens, the AMPP 2200 becomes a practical all-night light with sufficient battery reserve. Its included mount is quite secure, even on rough pavement. The trade-off is weight; at 211g, it’s the heaviest option on this list.

Pros: Exceptional max output, wide runtime range, secure mount, high-quality build

Cons: Heaviest light on this list; 2,200 lumens if overkill for those who don’t ride in complete darkness

Battery life: 4 to 80 hrs (front); 3 to 60 hrs (rear)

If you’re only looking for a pair of lights that will help you be seen, the Knog Frog combo could be the perfect fit. The front light output isn’t enough to illuminate a dark road, but not every triathlete wants to ride in the dark. Sometimes, you just want to be seen by drivers and cross-traffic, especially in low-light conditions. The combo’s battery life is fitting for the price point, and the pair is so light that you won’t even notice them. They come with a flexible silicone strap that wraps around virtually any tube shape, including aero bars. While they won’t light up a country road, the Knog Frog combo is great for being seen in the city, on the bike path, or on a foggy training loop.

Pros: Aero-bar compatible, extremely lightweight, very affordable, easy to use

Cons: 40 lumens won’t illuminate a dark road; not a standalone solution for night riding

Battery life: 16 hrs (day flash mode); 6 hrs (solid mode)

The Varia is a rear light that also functions as a vehicle radar. In terms of safety and security, it is one of the best bike lights on the market. When paired with a compatible Garmin head unit or Varia app, the light alerts you to vehicles approaching from behind, before you can even hear them. It is an incredibly useful safety feature, especially if you frequently ride in groups or on busy roads. If you get nervous riding on open roads, the Varia RTL515 could be the best option for you. While the light function itself isn’t anything special, the radar is the reason to buy it.

Pros: Vehicle radar is a game-changer on open roads; lightweight, impressive battery life, pairs with Garmin ecosystem

Cons: Expensive for a single rear light; radar requires a compatible head unit or phone mount

Battery life: 12 hrs constant; 30 hrs flash

In terms of bang for your buck, it’s hard to beat the Gravity Plus, which uses an accelerometer to detect braking and automatically increases brightness when you decelerate. It is effectively functioning as a brake light, and it is one of the cheapest options on this list. For triathletes who ride out of town, train with unpredictable stop-and-go conditions, or frequent group rides, the brake-sensing rear light is surprisingly effective. Runtime is excellent for a budget light, and you probably won’t even notice the added weight.

Pros: Brake-sensing technology, outstanding battery life, lightweight

Cons: 100 lumens is modest; a brighter light is necessary for riding in complete darkness

#8826. Cold, Dark, Rainy? The 10 Best Editor-Tested Indoor Bike Trainers Keep Your Training on Track

Our editors tested the best indoor bike trainers for winter miles, Zwift rides, and every budget.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. How we test gear.

Well, friends, it’s that time of year again. Colder temperatures and shorter daylight hours mean indoor riding season is right around the corner for many of us—if it hasn’t already arrived where you live. But thankfully, newer trainer tech and digital connectivity make those boring nights spent staring at your basement wall or garage door while endlessly spinning the pedals a thing of the past.

Smart trainers—some priced under $500—connect to Zwift and Rouvy, popular platforms that feature virtual worlds, group rides, and even organized races. Plus, lower prices on nicely-equipped indoor bikes mean you no longer have to wrestle with putting your bike on the trainer or ruining pricey components with sweat.

Our editors test trainers year-round, from budget-friendly units to the most advanced smart bike models currently available. We do workouts and ride a ton of base miles; some staff even compete at a high level in virtual racing leagues, giving us important feedback on trainer accuracy, stability, and durability.

The Wahoo Kickr Core 2 with Zwift Cog and Click is our Best Overall Indoor Trainer because it’s the perfect choice for most riders. It combines Wahoo’s excellent base-model direct-drive trainer with Zwift’s singlespeed cog and virtual shifting. The system sets up easily and works with almost any bike, regardless of gear range or number of speeds. (You can easily swap the Zwift Cog with a cassette if you don’t like the virtual gearing.) This enables multiple riders in a household to share one trainer, even if their bikes have different drivetrains or gearing.

I used the first-generation Kickr Core as my home setup for four years without any issues. Wahoo’s recent updates to the Core only make an already great smart trainer even better. Test Editor Dan Chabanov recently used the new Kickr Core 2 for three months after switching from the more expensive Kickr V6. He said, “Honestly, I can’t say I’ve noticed any kind of downgrade.”

On paper, the Kickr Core 2 has lower maximum wattage, less grade simulation, and slightly less claimed accuracy. In practice, the ride feel is almost identical on both models. Like the Kickr V6, the Core now features Wi-Fi (along with Bluetooth and ANT+) for smooth connectivity and faster data transmission for online events. “Truly, the only reason to opt for the pricier V6 is that it folds slightly smaller and is easier to move around,” Chabanov concluded.

The Zwift Cog uses virtual shifting to change gears instead of your bike’s shifters and derailleurs. Unfortunately, virtual shifting only works in Zwift. If you plan to ride without Zwift (or on another platform), purchase the Kickr Core 2 with a cassette.

Tired of putting your bike on the trainer every time you want to ride indoors?

Dedicated training bikes, such as the Zwift Ride, are a great option for indoor riding. This way, you have a bike on the trainer that’s always ready to ride. No more fumbling to remove your wheel or wearing down tires. The Ride’s adjustment range also makes it easy to set up and share with multiple riders in a household.

“After more than a year of heavy use by my wife and me, the Zwift Ride has proven to be a durable, impressively quiet alternative to abusing our 'good' bikes on a trainer, with excellent Zwift integration and easy adjustability for our multi-rider household,” said Senior Test Editor Matt Phillips.

Zwift’s recent updates addressed our criticisms of the original Ride. The V2 now fits more riders (4’10” to 6’6”), adds saddle adjustability, and increases the bar diameter. It also includes Zwift’s multi-position crank with lengths from 160mm to 175mm, which used to be a $100 upcharge.

If you ride indoors and want a dedicated setup that integrates with Zwift out of the box (and don’t want to spend thousands of dollars for a premium indoor bike), the Zwift Ride is an excellent option. Zwift sells the Ride Smart Frame alone (without a trainer) for $800 if you already have a direct-drive trainer.

Since launching in 2012, the Wahoo Kickr has consistently been one of the best indoor trainers and a favorite of Bicycling’s staff. While the sixth version of the venerable smart trainer is more of an update than a wholesale redesign, the changes help the Kickr rank ahead of other high-performance smart trainers.

The latest iteration features the same flywheel as the previous one, so the two units look virtually identical. As a result, both generations experience the same ride feel. The Kickr ramps up smoothly and correctly as you accelerate. Power accuracy is very good, and most riders will find the claimed 1-percent accuracy to be true.

Despite its high price and lack of cassette-sizing options, the latest Kickr is a solid choice. It’s the best option for performance-minded cyclists who push big watts or racers who require accuracy and improved connectivity for online events.

If you need a basic, budget-friendly trainer that gets the job done in a pinch—and offers compatibility with third-party apps like Zwift—the Tacx Boost Trainer Bundle is a solid option. With its magnetic roller, you can manually adjust resistance across ten levels. And because the Boost uses magnetic resistance instead of fluid or fans, it stays relatively quiet. The loudest sounds you’ll hear are your drivetrain and the tire on the roller.

The bundle includes a Garmin speed sensor and a front wheel block to keep your bike level while riding. It also folds up easily for compact storage. For an easy-to-use, low-cost, no-frills setup, this one covers the essentials.

The Saris Fluid2 is a good trainer at a reasonable price. This makes it a solid pick for riders who need something basic to keep up with their training plan on rainy days, rehab from injury, or get back into riding before heading outside onto the bike path, road, or trails.

The Fluid2’s wheel-on design means you don’t need to fumble with your drivetrain to set it up, and the fluid resistance provides a smooth, progressive ride feel. Although this version isn’t compatible with Zwift, Rouvy, or other online platforms, the Saris combo kit (for $40 more) includes a wheel sensor that adds connectivity. Also be sure to get an adaptor kit if your bike has a thru axle rear wheel.

Instead of buying that no-name $50 or $80 trainer, spend a little more for a proven trainer from a trusted brand. While it looks similar to Saris’ Fluid 2 (above), the Mag Plus uses a magnetic sensor to provide resistance instead of fluid. This saves a little money and gives you a linear feel (versus the Fluid’s progressive resistance). However, a big downside is that they tend to wear out tires pretty quickly, especially pricey, high-performance rubber.

Mag trainers have been around for decades (I’ve had several from different brands over the years); the tech hasn’t changed much and they don’t have any smart features. If you plan to ride Zwift or Rouvy, you need to install a wheel sensor. If you need a super basic trainer that gets the job done for only $100, the Mag Plus is your best bet.

The Neo 3M matches the Wahoo Kickr in power measurement (up to 2,200 watts with 1% accuracy) and maximum simulated gradient (up to 25%), but it has two unique features. The Neo generates its own electricity, so you can use it without external power (though it works best when plugged in). And, like an old-school Nintendo Rumble Pack, the Neo 3M vibrates to simulate a wide range of road surfaces—from gravel to cobblestones to concrete slab roads—when you’re riding Zwift.

Unlike other direct-drive trainers that use belts or rollers to transmit power, the Neo 3M uses a metal flywheel with magnets that interact with electrical coils to moderate resistance. Combined with the built-in motion plates, the trainer has an impressively realistic ride feel. However, the Neo 3M lacks a native high-speed data transfer mode or built-in Wi-Fi—a great feature for competitive virtual racing—but Garmin offers a separate adaptor.

The Wahoo Kickr Bike Pro is the indoor trainer of choice for riders seeking the best possible experience—and who have the space for a dedicated setup. At $4,000, it’s like investing in an extra bike that you can’t even ride outside. However, for many riders, the price is worth it since it’s always ready to go. You don’t need to install a bike or connect any devices. Plus, highly corrosive sweat and salt from trainer rides won’t damage your outside bike.

The Kickr Bike Pro adjusts to almost all bike fit measurements. Or, if you had a Guru, Retül, or Trek bike fit, you can plug the dimensions into the Wahoo app for more precise setup. Since the Bike uses virtual shifting, you can program it to any Shimano, SRAM, or Campagnolo drivetrain you want to ride. You can select the gear ratios and the number of teeth per cog.

The Kickr Bike Pro’s incredible ride feel comes from its high-tech flywheel with motor; it adds resistance while simulating the inertia of real-world riding. The Pro provides a coasting feel along with realistic braking and shifting. The system also features a piston-like mechanism that reflects virtual elevation changes by adjusting the angle between the bike and the ground (up to 20% incline and 15% decline).

If the Kickr Bike Pro’s $4,000 price tag is a little out of reach, check out the Kickr Bike Shift. It’s similar to the Pro in adjustment, but ditched the fancy flywheel and gradient-change feature—and it saves you almost $1,500.

Feedback’s Omnium Over-Drive is compact, lightweight (14 pounds), and sets up and breaks down fast. That’s why these portable trainers are ubiquitous in parking lots and team tents at bike races. These same traits also make it a great option for riders with small apartments or training while away from home.

However, this portable trainer isn’t light on features. Two 4-inch magnetic drums provide progressive resistance up to 1,050 watts (at 55 mph). Thanks to its height-adjustable fork mount and sliding base, the Over-Drive accommodates most bikes, wheel sizes, and quick-release or thru-axle configurations. Feedback includes a durable tote bag for storage under a bed, in your garage, or in a car trunk.

The trainer’s compact size makes it easy to carry on a plane as checked luggage (or in your bike bag)—I brought it along many times on trips to Asia and Europe. Plus, the Omnium’s quiet ride won’t disturb neighbors in a hotel room.

Wahoo’s unique-looking Kickr Rollr is a novel approach to indoor trainers. It’s a great option for those who need to install or remove their bike quickly. This makes it easy to use in a pinch, such as when an afternoon thunderstorm rolls in and threatens to cancel your training ride.

At the front, the Rollr features an A-shaped bracket that holds your bike’s front wheel with a tool-free clamp that accommodates tires up to 2.1 inches/53mm wide. At the back, the Rollr’s two drums cradle your bike’s rear tire, and an external flywheel adds resistance.

This design makes it quick and easy to put a bike on the Kickr Rollr, swap out multiple bikes, or share a trainer with other riders. However, we don’t recommend this trainer for riders who do a lot of out-of-the-saddle, high-intensity training or for users who regularly race on Zwift. (A direct-drive trainer will be better suited for these tasks.)

While the Rollr is adjustable for different wheelbases, the adjustment is limited and optimized for road bikes. This means long-wheelbase mountain bikes might not fit (most road or gravel bikes shouldn’t have any issues). Since the trainer doesn’t read power, you must have a power meter to use the Rollr’s smart features.

Direct-drivetrainers attach to your bike’s rear dropouts and replace your rear wheel with a resistance unit. These trainers are typically quieter than other systems, provide more accurate power readings, and are ideal for high-power efforts.

Friction trainers use a roller pressed against your bike’s rear tire. They’re lighter, (usually) more affordable, and more portable than other systems. However, friction trainers can be very noisy and wear out tires.

Rollers are a time-tested indoor riding platform. They use three drums (rollers) that you ride on, so they require balance. While some rollers have resistance, many don’t.

Smart bikes are dedicated indoor training bikes. These trainers are heavy and take up space, but they’re a great option if you have a bigger budget, are tired of taking your bike on/off the trainer, or don’t want to wreck your outdoor bike with sweat and salt.

Typically, a smart trainer is an indoor trainer that can wirelessly communicate power data with a training app on a smartphone or computer. Most smart trainers also work with virtual riding platforms like Zwift by automatically adjusting resistance to simulate changes in terrain.

The popularity of online riding platforms means most newer trainers are “smart” and will both transmit your data and adjust resistance. These features often add to the cost of a new trainer. But prices are falling; you can find connected trainers—such as the Saris M2—for less than $200.

If you want to try Zwift but don’t have a smart trainer, you can still log virtual miles using a Bluetooth speed sensor. Check out our guide to getting started here.

Compatibility: With axle attachment standards and widths frequently changing, check if the trainer you want offers different attachment options (such as thru-axle adaptors, or for direct-attachment trainers, free-hub options). Some trainers come with them. If yours doesn’t, you’ll need to purchase them separately. The Robert Axle Project is my go-to resource for replacement thru-axles and adapters.

Noise: While most manufacturers can get away with using words like “silent” and “virtually silent” to describe the noise level of their trainers, there are other factors to consider, such as the sound your bike’s drivetrain makes as you pedal, and if you use one, the fan that’s whirring away to keep you cool and simulate wind speeds. To get a better idea of how loud “silent” actually is, we used a decibel meter to record the noise levels of each trainer being ridden at 15 and 25 mph. Decibels ranged from 68 (comparable to a vacuum cleaner) to 85 (a diesel truck going 40 mph); the fan alone measured 71. To get an idea of how significant a seemingly minor jump in decibels can be, 70 is twice as loud as 60, and 80 is twice as loud as 70.‌

Stability: Trainer crashes are rare, but not unheard of when you’re going cross-eyed trying to beat your PR on a workout. Typically, the wider the trainer’s base, the more stable it will be. Many have a leveling feature for uneven surfaces.

As Deputy Editor, Tara Seplavy leads Bicycling’s product test team; after having previously led product development and sourcing for multiple bike brands, run World Championship winning mountain bike teams, wrenched at renowned bicycle shops in Brooklyn, raced everything from criteriums to downhill, and ridden bikes on six different continents (landing herself in hospital emergency rooms in four countries and counting). Based in Easton, Pennsylvania, Tara spends tons of time on the road and trail testing products. A familiar face at cyclocross races, crits, and bike parks in the Mid Atlantic and New England, on weekends she can often be found racing for the New York City-based CRCA/KruisCX team. When not riding a bike, or talking about them, Tara listens to a lot of ska, punk, and emo music, and consumes too much social media.

#8825. Essential Yoga Poses That Deliver Serious Knee Strengthening

The thing about practicing yoga for knee strengthening is you typically don’t know you need to do it until there’s an issue. YouTube yoga teacher Yoga With Kassandra takes you through a routine designed to emphasize the muscles that support knee strength and explains how to modify the poses to suit your needs.

Whether you’re wanting to build knee strength to enhance your everyday functionality or you’re recovery from a knee injury and finally at the point where you can practice yoga, you need strengthening exercises that support all the muscles that support and stabilize your knees. Basically, you want to work on the hip adductors, the quads, the glutes, the hamstrings.

The following poses literally work all of the muscles that contribute to knee stability. You’ll also get to play around a little with some dynamic movement and try some balancing exercises that help you understand how to properly engage the muscles that support the knee. Then you can take that awareness into other yoga poses as well as your everyday movements.

Regularly practicing this yoga for knee strength routine will help anyone build knee strength. I know from personal experience just how frustrating a knee injury can be, so if that applies to you, know that the more you dedicate time towards rehabilitating yourself, and the more diligent you are with your practices, the more likely you’ll feel a difference in your ease of movement. And remember that rest is equally as important as stretching and strengthening.

You will need a block or a block-like item for several of these poses. If you experience pain in any of the poses, slowly come out and skip ahead to the next pose. Always consult with your physician or physical therapist prior to introducing new exercises.

Start lying on your back and bring your feet about hip-distance apart and your heels pretty close toward your glutes. Place the block directly in between the inner thighs and squeeze the block as much as you possibly can. Then push down into all four corners of both feet and slowly lift first the pelvis off the mat, then the lower back, and then the mid back in Bridge Pose. The higher you lift, the harder it becomes to squeeze your block, but keep squeezing it anyway. This helps train your inner thighs, or adductor muscles, to contract. Building inner thigh power can also help you become better at balancing poses.

Take about 3 breaths here, pushing down through your big toes. Then exhale and slowly roll down, inch by inch. Move your block to the side.

From lying on your back, lift your right leg toward the sky and straighten it without locking your knee or hyperextending it. Interlace your fingers behind your right hamstrings. Instead of making this a passive stretch, push your leg against your palms as much as you can, and feel your arms resist. Keep pushing, pushing, pushing with your hamstrings. This should be challenging. You’ll also get a little arm workout. Try to keep your lower back neutral and close to the mat. Continue for a few more breaths.

You might find that your leg starts coming a little closer toward your chest, and that’s fine, but don’t force the stretch. Then release and switch legs.

Re-extend your right leg and bring your hands behind the back of your calf muscles. If that means you need to bend a little in your knee, that’s perfectly fine. If you can’t reach that far, bring your hands to the hamstrings again, but shift them closer to the knee, which creates a different sensation. Same thing, you want to push against your hands and resist. Then repeat on the other side.

This is not a yoga pose, but it’s absolutely amazing for your adductors. Grab your block and place it between your inner thighs again. Instead of keeping your heels close to you as in Bridge, walk your feet out so it feels almost as if your legs are almost straight and there’s about 6 inches between the mat and the backs of your knees.

Flex your feet, push your heels down into the mat, and see if you can squeeze your block and lift your hips off the mat. They’re only going to lift about an inch or so and that’s fine. This is an intense pose. You’re gonna feel it in your legs pretty much right away. If you don’t feel it, it’s because your knees are too bent and you need to straighten them a little more. Squeeze your block, push down into your heels, and try to drag your heels toward your shoulders. Hold here for a few more breaths. Then lower and move your block off to the side.

Come into Downward-Facing Dog. Normally I would suggest some Cat and Cow stretches before going into Down Dog, but if you’re recovering from knee issues you might not be able to apply bring your knees to the mat because of the pressure, so consider those stretches optional or take a seated version of them. You’re pushing into the heels here to stretch your hamstrings, lengthen your arms, and lengthen your spine.

Reach your right leg toward the sky in Three-Legged Dog, then step forward toward the top of the mat. Push down into your feet and come up into High Lunge. You want your feet hip-distance apart for stability. It’s find to bend your back knee if that feels more doable. It’s important that your front knee is going in the same direction as your toes and is stacked over your ankle. You don’t want the knee to be swaying to one side or jutting forward in front of your toes.

Bring your hands to your heart and keep your right knee bent and focus on its stability as you tilt your chest forward into a variation of Warrior 3. Keep the knee of your supporting leg bent as you reach your left leg back and find your balance.

As you inhale, push your right leg straight, and then exhale gently as you bend your right knee again. Think of this as almost like a one-legged squat. So inhale, straighten the leg. Exhale, bend the knee.

Continue for several breaths. Keep your right knee pointing straight over the second and third toes. Last one, inhale to straighten and hold here.

From Warrior 3, reach your left leg straight toward the ceiling and bring your chest toward your right thigh in Standing Splits. You might want to bring your block underneath your hands or fingertips.

Then exhale, bend both knees as much as you can, and see if you can bring your knees together to touch, so you’re in a little ball with your left foot hovering above the mat.

Then inhale, open back up into Standing Splits. Look at your right knee and make certain it’s not shifting to the right or the left. Do that once more.

Bend both knees and bring your left foot to the mat with your big toes together and your heels slightly apart in Chair Pose. If this creates tension in your lower back, you can keep your feet hip-distance apart. Rock your weight back into your heels and keep your tailbone reaching back and your thighs hugging the midline as if you were still squeezing that block. Stay here or reach your arms alongside your head.

Lean more weight onto your right leg, and see if you can pick up your left foot and step it back into your High Lunge. Then very carefully pivot the back foot almost parallel to the short side of the mat, keeping your shin and your knee facing the same direction, in Warrior 2. Your right knee is still bending. Squeezing the glutes helps press that right knee open as it points forward. Reach your arms straight out from your shoulders.

To work on strengthening, inhale as you straighten the front leg and bring your hands together in front of you, and then exhale back into Warrior 2 and reach your arms. Repeat several times. The goal is not to rush this but to do it with control. You want to really feel that knee tracking directly over the second and third toes and not wobbling.

Straighten your right leg, being careful not to lock or hyperextend your knees. Then shift forward into Triangle Pose and reach your left arm upward. Draw your left shoulder slightly back as you open across the chest.

From Triangle, look down at the floor and circle your hands to the mat. Step to Downward-Facing Dog.

Repeat these poses on your left side, starting with High Lunge and continuing to Dynamic Warrior 3, Standing Splits, Chair Pose, Dynamic Warrior 2, Triangle, and Down Dog.

From Down Dog, walk your feet to the top of the mat. Bend your knees a little, grab your block, and come all the way to standing. Come into Mountain Pose with the block in between your thighs, just as you did in Bridge Pose. Squeeze the block and hug in toward the midline. You can feel the adductors engage. Plant down firmly through all four corners of both feet.

As you inhale, stand a little taller. As you exhale, continue to squeeze your block as you lower yourself into Chair Pose. Repeat this movement about 5 times, moving slowly and steadily, continuing to squeeze the block. You might need to adjust your block a little.

Slowly fold forward in Standing Forward Bend. If you need to bend your knees, that’s perfectly fine. Even in this fold, can you squeeze your block? Then bend your knees a little more and release your block.

Slowly roll all the way up to standing. Notice how you feel as you attempt the pose, because if you’re still injured, the shape might not be accessible to you, and it’s fine to skip it. Lean onto your right foot, bend your left knee, and catch hold of the inner edge of your left foot behind you with your left hand. Keep your left hip and knee drawing inward toward the midline. So imagine you’re still squeezing your block in between your thighs. That is really important.

Reach your right arm forward. Instead of dipping the chest down and thinking of lifting the leg up, focus on pushing your foot into your palm. You’re not going super far forward in your Dancer Pose. You’re not working on flexibility, you’re working on strength, although you might feel an intense stretch along the front of your lifted quads.

To help with balance, you can always practice within arm’s reach of a chair or a wall so that you can reach out if needed for extra steadiness.

Then release and repeat on your other leg, foot into the right hand.

Make your way onto your belly on the mat. The shape of this pose is very similar to Dancer, so if this isn’t working for you, work on Locust Pose. If you want to do Bow Pose, bend your knees and see if you can catch hold of your feet and imagine you still have the block in between the inner upper thighs. Squeeze in and start to push the feet against your hands.

If you’re not doing Bow Pose, then bring your arms alongside your body, palms facing the mat, and slowly lift your feet and legs and chest off the mat Focus your gaze forward and down to keep the back of your neck long. Hold here or slowly release and then lift several times.

Flip over onto your back. Grab your block, lift your hips, slide your block underneath your pelvis, and just let yourself settle here. Slow down your breath and start to unwind.

When you’re ready, press into your feet, lift your pelvis, and move your block to the side before lowering yourself down. Maybe you draw your knees toward your belly and bring your arms underneath your calves and stay still or rock a little side to side.

Extend your arms and legs, close your eyes, and notice how you feel now as opposed to when you first started this practice. Let yourself settle into this space.

When you’re ready, begin to lengthen your breath and wiggle your fingers and toes. You can reach your arms up overhead, take a big stretch, and roll onto one side. Come up to take a seat, sitting up tall, maybe closing your eyes for a moment.

Thank you so much for doing this knee-strengthening sequence with me. I hope that it gave you some ideas as to how you can strengthen your knees.

#8824. Replacing Your Bike Chain Is Easier Than You Think—Here’s How to Do It at Home

A step-by-step home repair guide to measuring, removing, and installing a bike chain.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. How we test gear.

Replacing a chain is a great way for someone to tap into their home bike maintenance potential. It’s a pretty straightforward process once you’re used to it, especially if you have the existing chain to measure from. I typically recommend being familiar with a few skills before diving into replacing your chain. The first skill to know is adjusting your front and rear derailleurs. The second is knowing how to use a chain checker. The third is being familiar with a pre bike check. This last one is especially helpful because it will allow you to run through the bike to see if there are any other issues before diving into swapping out your chain. Again, these skills are not required skills to replace a chain, but having some familiarity with the basic mechanics addressed above will only help make this process easier. Here we’ll go through the tools you’ll need and the basic process to replace your chain at home.

How often should you replace your chain? Before answering that question, it helps to understand the process of chain wear. As your chain ages, each link’s internal bushings slowly lengthen. In turn, your now-longer chain puts added pressure on your cassette cogs and chainring teeth, causing them to wear faster. This also hampers shifting quality.

To avoid this accelerated wear of your cassette and chainrings, a general rule of thumb is to replace your bike’s chain every 2,000 miles. Mind you, this is just a starting point. No two chains will wear at exactly the same rate because no two riders treat their chains the same.

These differences in riding style are why it is best to periodically use a chain wear measuring tool to determine the condition of your chain. With the tool in hand, apply pressure to a pedal so the top of the chain is taut, and then place the measuring tool in place on the chain as shown in the video above and read the results. Indicators on the tool will tell you whether it’s time to replace your chain.

Cutting a new bike chain to the correct length for installation and removing a damaged link for an on-trail chain repair are essentially the same job. Make life easier by using a full-size tool at home, and save the compact tool for midride fixes.

To start, you’ll need to pick up the right size chain for your bike. We’re not talking about the length of the chain here (you’ll address that later), but width. This is dictated by the number of cogs on your cassette; a six-speed bike uses the same width chain as an eight-speed, but a nine-speed needs something different, and so on. (Check out Park Tool’s chain compatibility guide for more on this.) The easiest way to ensure you get the right chain is to buy the same kind of chain that came on your bike. If you decide to go with a different chain, it’s best to get one from the same manufacturer.

If your chain has a master link such as a Shimano Quick Link or SRAM PowerLock, use a pair of master link pliers to compress the link and undo it. (If it’s a newer chain, you might be able to do this with your hands.)

If there isn’t a master link, remove the chain using the chain breaker tool. Back out the tool’s pin to make room and fit a chain link into the outer slot, and line up the tool’s pin with a pin on the chain. Tighten the tool until its pin puts light pressure on the chain’s connecting pin. Crank the handle, making sure the tool’s pin stays straight. If it twists, stop and realign everything so as not to bend the tool’s pin. If you bend it, most tools have replaceable pins available; some even come with one inside the handle. Then push the pin far enough through so you can remove the extra links.

Remove the chain from your bike. Then, measure out the length of your new chain to match the length of your old chain, taking into account the master link. Remove any excess links from the new chain using the chain breaker tool, and install the master link. Thread the new chain onto your bike’s cassette and chainring and connect the ends with the master link, making sure the link is secure and locked in place.

When she’s not out riding her mountain bike, Jessica is an editor for Popular Mechanics. She was previously an editor for Bicycling magazine.
